title: Acute onset anarthria in a 7-year-old patient as a presentation of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis: A rare clinical and radiological entity
case_prompt:
A 7-year-old boy was brought to the pediatric emergency department with sudden inability to speak (anarthria), a mildly open and stiff mouth, and lethargy associated with low-grade fever. Two weeks earlier he had viral tonsillitis; there was no recent vaccination. He had normal psychomotor development and no relevant family history. 

On examination, temperature was 37.9°C; heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure were normal. He was conscious and followed commands but could not articulate speech. Neck stiffness was present, with negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs. There were no sensory or limb motor deficits; muscle strength was 5/5. Masseter rigidity prevented jaw movement. Deep tendon reflexes were brisk, and plantar responses were normal. Cranial nerves other than the trigeminal nerve were intact. Coordination, gait, and all other systemic exams were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and C-reactive protein, were normal. Noncontrast head CT was unremarkable. A lumbar puncture showed 5 white blood cells/µL, glucose 28 mg/dL, and protein 79 mg/dL. Empiric ceftriaxone and acyclovir were started; antibiotics were discontinued when CSF showed no infection, and acyclovir was continued.

On hospital day 2, his speech impairment persisted; he became obtunded, developed rigidity in all four limbs, and quadriparesis (muscle strength 3/5), with preservation of only ocular movements. Brain MRI revealed asymmetrical supratentorial lesions: ovoid, poorly marginated areas of increased signal on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences involving bilateral central white matter, cortical gray matter, and basal ganglia, with no enhancement on pre- or post-contrast T1-weighted images.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Consideration of meningoencephalitis — “CSF analysis was negative and did not reveal any sign of inflammation” ruled out an infectious process.  
2. Consideration of multiple sclerosis — “features typically found in ADEM and missing in MS include deep gray matter and cortical involvement, bilateral and poorly marginated diffuse lesions,” whereas MS shows Dawson’s fingers and black holes.  
3. Consideration of clinically isolated syndrome — “clinical isolated syndrome include optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, hemiparesis… and the absence of encephalopathy,” unlike this patient who had encephalopathy.  
4. Consideration of neuromyelitis optica — “the presence of anti–aquaporin-4 antibodies is highly evocative of it and could rule out ADEM diagnosis,” but the presentation lacked optic neuritis or myelitis.
